name: Fascism in Europe
summary: The scholarship on the interwar European movements describes a revolutionary ultranationalism of national rebirth: the nation and its leader above individual rights, a single mass party with a militia, extreme elitism and the leader principle, and a positive valuation of violence and war. It defines itself against liberalism, communism and conservatism, subordinates the economy to the state while keeping private property, and differs between movements on corporatism, religion, race and expansion.
scope: The classic interwar European fascist movements (Italian Fascism, German National Socialism and the movements modelled on or akin to them), as the comparative scholarship defines them: Payne's typological description, which he derives from the interwar European movements and not from a presumed category of regimes, with Gentile's ten-point definition he quotes, Paxton's mobilizing passions and Griffin's palingenetic ultranationalism. Where the two regimes that held power (Fascist Italy, Nazi Germany) acted alike, their record answers (Payne's account of their laws and policies); where they differ, or the sources are silent, the answer is null. Post-1945 neofascism, and fascist movements outside Europe, are other subjects, as are the authoritarian right regimes (Franco, Salazar, Vichy) that Payne and Griffin distinguish from fascism.

furtherReading.title: Payne, A History of Fascism, 1914-1945 (full text)
furtherReading.note: The standard comparative history of the European movements, with the typological description of what they shared.

furtherReading.title: Paxton, The Five Stages of Fascism
furtherReading.note: A short scholarly account of fascism's mobilizing passions and how the movements developed.

furtherReading.title: Griffin, Staging the Nation's Rebirth
furtherReading.note: Griffin sets out fascism as palingenetic ultranationalism and compares the Italian and German regimes.

sources.author: Stanley G. Payne

sources.author: Stanley G. Payne
sources.usedFor: The record of Fascist Italy and Nazi Germany in power: banned parties and unions, censorship, decree rule, racial laws, youth mobilization, autarky, rearmament and wars of expansion.

sources.author: Robert O. Paxton
sources.usedFor: Fascism's mobilizing passions: group primacy over every right, victimhood, decadence, leader, violence.

sources.author: Roger Griffin
sources.usedFor: Fascism as palingenetic ultranationalism, opposed to liberalism, socialism and conservatism; the institutions it implies.

sources.usedFor: Ties the alias: the same collection of essays on the European movements was published as European Fascism (1968) and as Fascism in Europe (1981).

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Payne lists the militarization of politics and normatized military virtues as defining fascist features.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: Gentile's definition quoted by Payne includes a police apparatus that prevents, controls and represses dissidence, even by organized terror.

arms-reduction.rationale: Payne records heavy German rearmament from 1936 and the Italian arms industry expanded under autarchy.

class-collaboration.rationale: Payne's typology gives fascism a multiclass, integrated national economic structure, and Gentile's definition he quotes seeks collaboration of the productive sectors under the regime.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Payne lists anticommunism among the fascist negations and says fascist ideology rejected economic determinism, whether of Manchester or Marx.

clerical-rule.rationale: Payne says fascism was secular and relegated supernatural religion to a secondary role or none at all in its civic religion.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Payne notes the fascist valuation of continuing violent struggle along the lines of extreme Social Darwinism as necessary for the health of national society.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Payne reports that most fascist movements espoused corporatism, but that German National Socialism, the most developed form, explicitly rejected formal corporatism.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Payne says all fascist movements were highly ethnicist, holding the potential for doctrines of inherent collective superiority of their nations.

defeat-communism.rationale: Payne lists anticommunism among the three fascist negations, and Griffin says fascism is anti-Marxist and rejects all forms of socialism.

democracy-best.rationale: Payne records Mussolini dismissing parliament and building a dictatorship, and Hitler governing by decree under the 1933 Enabling Act, with the opposition crushed.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Payne records that the Italian Law for the Defense of the Race forbade mixed marriages in 1938 and that Nazi racial purification segregated the Jews.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Payne says the fascist organic society made a place for women but with male predominance and an extreme stress on the masculine principle.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Payne says fascism was basically secular and post-religious, its transcendence immanent and this-worldly.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Paxton's first mobilizing passion of fascism is the primacy of the group, toward which one has duties superior to every right.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Payne records the Italian special legal measures against subversion and Special Tribunal after 1926 and the German decree powers and mass arrests of 1933.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Payne records Italy's military alliance with Germany, the 1939 Pact of Steel binding Italy to go to war whenever Germany did.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Payne records the Nazi segregation and exclusion of Jews from 1933 and the Italian regime's 1938 laws removing Jews from institutions and banning mixed marriages, so both regimes denied equal rights before the law.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Payne names the fascist rejection of rationalism, materialism and egalitarianism, and Griffin says fascism rejects equality as undermining a healthy national hierarchy.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Payne calls all fascist movements highly ethnicist as well as extremely nationalist, and Gentile's definition makes the nation an ethnic and moral community.

free-trade.rationale: Payne records the permanent Italian policy of autarchy to cut foreign competition from 1936 and the Nazi Four Year Plan geared to self-sufficiency.

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: Payne makes extreme stress on the masculine principle and male dominance a defining feature of fascism, and Paxton lists natural leaders as always male.

gradual-change.rationale: Payne calls fascism revolutionary and Griffin says it is anti-conservative and aims at a new order rather than a gradual reform of the old.

harm-principle.rationale: Gentile's definition quoted by Payne has a totalitarian primacy of politics integrating the individual into the national community, with persecution of those outside it.

independent-unions.rationale: Payne records that the Italian regime granted exclusive recognition to Fascist unions in 1925 and froze others out, and that Hitler's police occupied trade union offices in 1933 and the Labor Front replaced the unions.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Paxton lists duties to the group superior to every right, whether universal or individual, and Payne's organic society gives the group precedence over individual rights.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Griffin says fascism is not anti-modernist and many forms embrace modern technology and industrial civilisation when integrated into the national order.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Payne says fascism presupposed a post-Christian, secular, immanent frame of reference and displaced supernatural religion.

leader-cult.rationale: Gentile's definition quoted by Payne crowns the hierarchy with a leader invested with sacred charisma, and Paxton lists a national chieftain who alone incarnates the group's destiny.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Payne says the shared fascist economic aim was a highly regulated national economy under extensive governmental control, subordinating economic issues to the state.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Payne says fascist ideology was based on vitalism and idealism and rejected economic determinism, whether of Manchester or Marx.

military-organisation-revolutionary-part.rationale: Payne lists the militarization of political relationships with a mass party militia as a defining organizational feature of fascist movements.

military-superiority.rationale: Payne records the Four Year Plan and tripling of German military spending from 1936 and the Italian state's drive to expand the arms industry under autarchy.

more-religion-public.rationale: Payne calls fascism basically post-religious and secular, while Paxton says religion would play a larger part in some national variants.

nation-first.rationale: Payne defines fascism as revolutionary ultranationalism and Griffin as palingenetic ultranationalism, with the nation's interest above all other claims.

national-rebirth.rationale: Payne defines fascism as revolutionary ultranationalism for national rebirth, Griffin as palingenetic ultranationalism, and Paxton lists dread of decadence.

natural-rulers.rationale: Payne makes extreme elitism part of the fascist definition, and Paxton lists the authority of natural leaders throughout society.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: Payne lists anticommunism as a defining negation and the aim of ending large-scale capitalism's autonomy, while rejecting economic determinism whether of Manchester or Marx.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: Payne says fascist doctrine valued violence positively as an end as well as a means, which an absolute ban on killing contradicts.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Payne has fascism subordinating the economy to the state and building a regulated, totalitarian-leaning state, and Gentile's definition widens state intervention.

one-party-rule.rationale: Payne records that all other parties were banned in Italy in 1926 and that the NSDAP was declared the sole political party of Germany on July 14, 1933.

open-borders.rationale: Griffin says fascist nationality is redefined in exclusive historical, cultural or ethnic categories and liberal citizenship rejected.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Payne records that Italy's parliament was reduced to rubber-stamping decree laws and replaced in 1928 by a corporative chamber, and that the Reichstag handed Hitler decree power in 1933.

party-controls-media.rationale: Payne records censorship introduced in Italy in 1925 and the German press consolidated under strict censorship under Goebbels' Reich Chamber of Culture.

patriotic-education.rationale: Payne records the Nazi overhaul of the school curriculum and Hitler Youth indoctrination of 82 percent of young males by 1939 as major goals of the regime.

person-over-state.rationale: Paxton says fascism places duties to the group above every individual right, and Griffin says it has the individual subsume personality in the national community.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Paxton places dread of the group's decadence and its identity at the core of fascism, and Griffin says it seeks national rebirth from decadence, venerating a mythicised national history.

property-fundamental.rationale: Payne reports the movements held private property inherent to individual freedom, yet subordinated it to the state with extensive regulation and aimed to end the autonomy of large-scale capital, so the family's words point both ways.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Payne says fascist movements kept the principle of private property but subordinated economic issues to the state and the greater well-being of the nation.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Payne records Nazi segregation of Jews and Italian separate Jewish schools and the removal of Jews from institutions in 1938.

recall-officials.rationale: Gentile's definition quoted by Payne has a political system organized as a hierarchy of functions named from the top, crowned by the leader.

recallable-delegates.rationale: Gentile's definition quoted by Payne has a hierarchy of functions named from the top, and Payne says fascists deferred to the leader's creative function rather than to a party line.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Payne says what fascist movements had in common was ending the autonomy of large-scale capitalism and major industry under extensive governmental control and regulation.

restore-past-order.rationale: Payne says fascist doctrine did not represent a reversion to traditional values, and Griffin says it is antitraditional and aims at a new order.

sacred-nation.rationale: Payne says fundamental to fascism was a new civic religion of the movement and nation, and Griffin describes myths and rituals replacing individualism with a transcendental community.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Paxton puts duties to the group above individual rights, and Payne says fascism rejected materialism and prudential egotism.

separated-powers.rationale: Payne records the Italian parliament reduced to rubber-stamping decree laws, a special tribunal over political cases and Mussolini answerable only to the king, and the German Enabling Act giving Hitler power to govern by decree.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: Payne says the fascist organic notion of society gave the male's rights predominance and made male chauvinism a defining feature.

small-step-social-reform.rationale: Payne's typology has fascism anticonservative and revolutionary, aiming to transcend right-wing conservatism and create a new authoritarian state.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Payne lists the creation of a new nationalist authoritarian state not based on traditional models, and Gentile's definition has the regime destroying parliamentary democracy.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Payne says fascism sought a secular form of transcendence through a civic religion that binds the nation in a common faith.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Payne says fascist movements subordinated economic issues to the state and the nation's well-being, with extensive governmental control and regulation of the economy.

state-harmful.rationale: Payne's typology has fascism creating a new nationalist authoritarian state and Gentile's definition makes politics primary over the individual.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Payne records Italy and Germany forming the Axis and signing the Pact of Steel military alliance.

strong-leader.rationale: Payne says all fascist movements came to espouse variants of the Fuhrerprinzip and his typology lists an authoritarian, charismatic, personal style of command.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Payne records opposition deputies barred and parties banned in Italy, a special tribunal for political offenses, and the Nazi outlawing of the Communists and Socialists with about a hundred thousand arrests in 1933.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Payne records that Italy made autarchy permanent policy from 1936, reducing market forces and foreign competition, and that Nazi Germany pursued autarky under the Four Year Plan.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Payne records the Italian conquest of Ethiopia and occupation of Albania and the Nazi annexations of Austria, the Sudetenland and Polish territory.

total-state.rationale: Gentile's definition quoted by Payne has a totalitarian primacy of politics, but Payne cautions that fascist movements never projected a doctrine centralised enough for complete totalitarianism.

uniformed-youth.rationale: Payne records that the Hitler Youth organized 82 percent of males aged fourteen to eighteen by 1939 and that mobilization and indoctrination of youth were major Nazi goals.

universal-morality.rationale: Griffin says fascism repudiates the principles of universal human rights and the rationalist tradition of the Enlightenment.

war-builds-character.rationale: Payne says fascism positively values violence and tends to normatize war and the military virtues, and Paxton lists the beauty of violence and will in a Darwinian struggle.

women-suffrage.rationale: Payne says fascist society was organic with a place for women but with the male's rights predominant, and Paxton lists the authority of natural leaders, always male.

workers-nation.rationale: Griffin says fascism rejects socialism because its materialism, internationalism and equality are held to undermine a healthy national identity.

notes: Themes searched in Payne's full text, Paxton and Griffin: economy and labour, party and parliament, leader and elites, violence and war, empire and alliances, race and nation, women and family, religion and secularism, youth and education, culture and modernity. Payne's regime chapters answer only where Italy and Germany acted alike; religion, corporatism, empire and race differ between movements, so those are split or null. Britannica was not opened (blocked) and Griffin's The Nature of Fascism is lending-only, so Griffin is cited through his open chapter. The Italian and German primary texts (Doctrine of Fascism, Mein Kampf) were not used: Payne and Paxton treat early programmes as poor guides to later policy, and a single movement's texts do not answer for the family.
